Oct 15 : Thoma Bravo-owned cybersecurity company Proofpoint will buy data security firm Varonis Systems in all-cash deal valued at about $6.3 billion, the companies said on Thursday. Under the agreement, Varonis shareholders will receive $49.75 per share in cash, representing a premium of 52 per cent over Varonis' closing stock price on June 22, the day before initial speculation about a potential sale, according to the companies. Reuters reported in September that Proofpoint was in discussions to acquire Varonis Systems. Miami-based Varonis offers cybersecurity services, including data classification on cloud storage systems and employee behavior tracking. Its shares were up about 2 per cent in extended trading. Thoma Bravo in 2021 agreed to acquire Proofpoint, which sells software that helps companies guard against cyberattacks, valuing the firm at about $12.3 billion in the take-private deal.

Oct 15 : CoreWeave's mounting debt is raising fresh concerns about the AI boom, as investors question whether demand can justify the billions being borrowed to build data centres. Shares and bonds of the Nvidia-backed company have tumbled despite its CEO's assurances of a strong contract backlog, fueling a broader selloff in technology stocks. Here is why investors are worried and what its troubles could mean for the industry. WHAT DOES COREWEAVE DO?

CoreWeave rents out computing power from Nvidia processors to companies developing and running AI, including Microsoft and OpenAI. It is one of the leading "neocloud" providers, a group of newer cloud companies that are growing rapidly to meet demand for scarce and expensive AI chips. These neocloud companies give customers access to computing power without requiring them to build their own data centers. However, supplying such capacity requires heavy upfront investment in chips and infrastructure, often financed with debt. WHAT IS ITS FINANCIAL SITUATION? The company, which has never turned a profit, has about $50 billion in debt, according to data compiled by LSEG. It raised its annual capital spending forecast by $4 billion in August to between $35 billion and $39 billion. Analysts expect revenue of nearly $13 billion this year and a loss of $2.13 billion. The yields on its bonds due in 2031, which are rated junk, have spiked to about 16 per cent, while the cost of insuring its debt against default has climbed to about 1,000 basis points, reflecting growing concern among creditors. CEO Mike Intrator told employees in an internal memo seen by Reuters that its deal backlog more than covers its debt obligations. The company had a $104.2 billion revenue backlog at the end of the second quarter, followed by more than $25 billion in new commitments early in the third quarter. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has also downplayed the concerns, saying CoreWeave's financial strength is improving and he sees no need to backstop it. The chip giant has agreed to buy unsold CoreWeave capacity through April 2032. WHY IT COULD BE A CANARY IN THE COAL MINE CoreWeave's business depends on two things: demand for AI computing and lenders' willingness to finance the infrastructure supplying it. But a selloff in its shares suggests a lack of confidence among investors in the latter, even as the company cites strong demand. The concern is not that AI demand will collapse, but that higher borrowing costs could make the business harder to sustain if demand were to weaken sharply. "It looks more like investors questioning how the build-out is being funded than a sudden collapse in appetite for AI computing," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group. "CoreWeave is quickly becoming the AI trade's canary in the coal mine," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. WHY ARE MARKETS FRETTING? Investors are questioning whether AI revenue can grow fast enough to cover the cost of building and financing the infrastructure. CoreWeave has to spend heavily upfront before it can collect the revenue from its contracts. Higher interest rates could drive up financing costs and further squeeze returns. The hardware itself poses another risk. Chips lose value as newer generations arrive, pushing providers to spend even more to replace them. The concerns, however, go beyond CoreWeave. US technology giants are expected to spend more than $700 billion on AI infrastructure this year. THE DOWNSIDE SCENARIO One potential consequence would be a broader financing squeeze, with lenders demanding higher returns or becoming less willing to fund other AI projects. That could force providers to scale back expansion, curbing equipment purchases and affecting the computing capacity customers expect. A setback could also deepen doubts that the AI investment frenzy is outpacing returns, piling further pressure on technology stocks. The impact of the fallout would depend on how the business is reorganized, and CoreWeave's ties to major technology companies do not, by themselves, mean its failure would trigger a wider financial crisis. WHO ELSE BEARS THE RISK? Gartner estimates about 80 per cent of neoclouds could shut down by 2030, warning that expected AI revenue will not support profitable returns on all planned infrastructure spending. Neocloud rivals Nebius, Applied Digital and Iren have fallen in the recent selloff. The cost of default protection has risen for SoftBank, which is betting heavily on OpenAI. Meanwhile, spreads for Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Nvidia have also reached records, although they have risen much more slowly than CoreWeave's. However, these companies also have larger cash flows and stronger balance sheets.

Source: Reuters

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 15 : Amazon unveiled two new devices on Thursday for listening to and recording people's information throughout the day to offer calendar reminders and other AI-driven insights under the Bee brand it acquired last year. Frontier is a bracelet and Eclipse is a brick that resembles a portable magnetic charger. Users attach the Eclipse to their smartphones. The devices aggregate information from calendars, apps and other data throughout the day, Amazon said.  The Frontier bracelet costs $75 and the Eclipse $100, Amazon said. "They listen to your whole day," said Amazon devices chief Panos Panay at the TechCrunch Disrupt conference in San Francisco. "It reminds you of the conversations you had, it reminds you of to-dos that you may have had, it tells you that you have some action items that you committed to other people."

The devices can also connect to Alexa+, Amazon's subscription generative AI voice service. Amazon's Bee will face competition in AI wearables, notably Meta's Muse Charm, a pendant using the company's latest agentic AI software, and its eyeglasses with cameras and other sensors. A host of startups have also developed similar devices, designed to record conversations and take action on behalf of users. Oct 15 : Anthropic has given nonprofit METR employee-level access to its systems and is in talks with others including Hugging Face, as AI companies pitch external evaluators as a way to safely advance the technology without slowing its development. The developer of Claude models is also working with biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio and Accenture's AI business Faculty as evaluators, it said in a blog post on Thursday. Reuters exclusively reported earlier this week that Anthropic and OpenAI had sought significant control over what outside reviewers could publish, concerned that the findings could leak trade secrets. A person familiar with the matter told Reuters that talks with Anthropic had evolved recently, with the company becoming more open in negotiations.

A key sticking point between evaluators and AI labs is that information the companies might consider crucial intellectual property can also be relevant to assessing a model's risks, leading to disputes and redactions, a separate person familiar with the discussions told Reuters. Experts have also said the independence of evaluators is a concern, as Anthropic and OpenAI choose who gets to carry out the reviews. The outcome of the talks will help determine how the world scrutinizes a technology that some of its creators warn may be advancing beyond humanity's ability to manage. THE METR TIE-UP Anthropic said on Thursday six employees of METR — or Model Evaluation and Threat Research — have company hardware, office space and access to internal systems roughly equivalent to its risk assessment teams. However, customer data, legally privileged information and model architecture will remain off limits. The company said it cannot veto METR's findings on risks, incidents and practices, but can require narrowly defined redactions. METR can also publicly question those redactions without revealing the withheld information. "In line with our transparency policies, our report will openly describe the scope, access, and other limitations of our work," METR said. The nonprofit had proposed on Wednesday that developers allow private staff interviews, timely publication of assessments and transparency about access limits and redactions. Anthropic said its other evaluator partnerships are at an early stage, with more limited access and publication rights.  The company is developing three tiers of access. Evaluators at the first level will conduct narrowly scoped investigations and need approval to publish. Those at the second will receive more information and can publish without approval, subject to redactions evaluators can publicly challenge. The third, used by METR, provides employee-like access with similar publication rights to the second tier. SecureBio is in the first tier and is reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of Anthropic's August risk report, having published a pilot review of the previous report. Anthropic said it would consider expanding SecureBio's access and publication rights after the review. Anthropic also announced last month that it is working on a tie-up with Faculty covering model evaluations, adversarial testing and assessments of whether models behave as intended, among other areas.

Oct 15 : Skydance's CNN, the Financial Times, Axios and other publishers joined Google's AI news program to license their content for generative AI features and explore ways to drive audience engagement. The search-engine giant said on Thursday that the program, which started as a pilot last year with partners like The Washington Post, now includes more than 400 publications globally. The deal marks CNN's first partnership since Paramount Skydance completed its acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, as CEO David Ellison seeks to position the combined company as a technology-driven media business. As part of these agreements, publishers will provide enhanced content rights, allowing Google to develop new AI features, while Google will pay participating news organizations for their content. Financial terms were not disclosed.

WASHINGTON, Oct 15 : Nvidia and Apple each committed $25 million for US President Donald Trump's planned White House ballroom, according to a Washington Post report on Thursday that showed $333 million in private donations for the project. The Adelson family, longtime financial supporters of Trump and his Republican Party, committed $25 million as well, as did billionaire Charles Ergen, co-founder and chairman of telecommunications company Dish Network, the report added.  The president himself is not on the list, according to the Post. Reuters has not verified the report. The White House said it would not release information about the donors, who spokesman Davis Ingle said "represent a wide array of great American companies."

Nvidia said it was proud to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves Americans. "As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," a spokesperson said. Apple declined to comment. The scale of the ballroom project and the administration’s handling of fundraising and disclosures have drawn criticism from watchdog groups and legal experts, who say they raise questions about transparency, donor influence and adherence to longstanding ethics and oversight norms. "The secrecy is a huge problem," said Eric Petry of the Brennan Center for Justice. "When people with business before the government can give millions to the president's pet project, and the public can't see who or how much, there's no way to tell whether they're buying access or favors." Federal contractors including Lockheed Martin Corp, Microsoft Corp and Palantir Technologies Inc all gave $10 million, the Post reported. The companies did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump initially said he and wealthy donors would pay for the estimated $400 million project, but he later unsuccessfully sought $1 billion from Congress for an underground bunker and security features to harden the facility. The Post reported that the "vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government" and that half the total came from companies or executives of firms that have had federal government contracts in Trump's second White House term. The planned ballroom is among several projects Trump is pursuing in his efforts to remake Washington with sweeping, unilateral changes that his opponents have challenged in court and called a power grab. The US Supreme Court, in a 5-4 ruling in August, allowed Trump to continue construction of the ballroom while he challenges a judicial order that would halt much of the development. In a dissent, Chief Justice John Roberts said the project was "likely unlawful." The ballroom, which Trump has said will seat 1,000 guests, has faced public backlash. Preservationists and opponents say Trump exceeded his authority by demolishing the historic East Wing, which housed the first lady's offices and the White House movie theater, to make room for the structure. Trump says a planned 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) White House ballroom will include bomb shelters, medical facilities, defenses against drones and missiles and other security features. Confronted with criticism of the project, his administration now says the facility is needed for national security, an argument the president has also made about a proposed triumphal arch.

Oct 15 : The bones of a Neanderthal from a cave in Iraq's Kurdistan region are offering evidence of both violence and compassion in the closest evolutionary cousins of our species, exhibiting a wound apparently from a fatal spear attack as well as signs of an earlier nonfatal injury that may have elicited kindly care. Researchers have discovered at Shanidar Cave in the Zagros Mountains of northern Iraq a partial skeleton of a Neanderthal, aged in the mid-40s, that included a left shoulder blade, or scapula, with a circular hole six-tenths of an inch (15 mm) wide indicative of a deeply penetrating stab. The bones of this individual, who they call Shanidar A, were unearthed from under about 25 feet (7.5 meters) of rocks and sediment inside the cave and date to about 75,000 years ago. The researchers were unable to determine Shanidar A's sex. The researchers said the injury's shape suggests it was caused by a forceful thrust using a sharpened wooden spear, a type of weapon Neanderthals are known to have used, rather than a spear with a stone tip. It was a weapon employed in hunting large mammals that were an important food source.

"The spear would have gone through the skin and major muscles, especially the pectoralis, as well as the ribcage and muscles between the ribs, and the lung," said biological anthropologist Emma Pomeroy of the University of Cambridge in England, lead author of the study published on Thursday in the journal Scientific Reports. "The location could be like the kind of 'heart shot' hunters use to kill animals quickly by puncturing the heart, but that is a bit speculative. We do see heart shots as a hunting strategy both today and in the archaeological record. Neanderthals would have known this would lead to a quick death," Pomeroy said. University of Cambridge archaeologist and study co-author Graeme Barker, who has led Shanidar Cave excavations since 2015, said the likeliest scenario is interpersonal violence. The researchers said the violence probably occurred either between members of a particular Neanderthal group or between members of rival Neanderthal groups, calling a Homo sapiens attack or an accidental injury less likely. The researchers found shards of bone displaced by the weapon. The injury indicated that the spear entered from above with a downward trajectory, penetrating the left chest cavity from the front and traveling through the body before punching the hole in the scapula, causing quick death. ANOTHER INJURY In addition to the scapula, the researchers found some ribs, a nearly complete right hand and seven teeth, mostly from the front of the lower jaw, belonging to Shanidar A. The teeth bore evidence that this Neanderthal had survived brutal injury at least a year before death — a blow to the face resulting in front teeth being smashed and lost. One tooth was split, with half remaining rotated in the mouth and others pushed out of position. "The pain would have been extreme, and basic needs like eating and drinking would have been difficult, perhaps meaning Shanidar A needed food mashing and being able to rest. It's likely that Shanidar A did need some care from members of the group for some basic needs during recovery," Pomeroy said. Shanidar A was one of five Neanderthals, four adults and one infant, whose bodies were carefully tucked behind a rock pillar in the cave in a burial cluster within a generation or so of each other. The cave was occupied by Neanderthals for tens of thousands of years as a seasonal campsite, and later by Homo sapiens. Neanderthals were more robustly built than Homo sapiens, with larger brows. They lived as hunter-gatherers and inhabited Eurasia from the Atlantic coast to the Ural Mountains from about 400,000 years ago until a bit after 40,000 years ago, disappearing after Homo sapiens became established in the region. The two species interbred, with modern non-African human populations bearing residual Neanderthal DNA. The cave, overlooking the Great Zab river valley, has been a source of information about Neanderthals since the 1950s, with Shanidar A now offering new insight into their behavior. "We see evidence of two contrasting facets of human nature – care and violence – juxtaposed in the same individual," Pomeroy said. "We see evidence all around us today that violence and care are both aspects of how we humans behave, and we see this here in Shanidar A, too. Neanderthals were like us in many respects, both the good and the bad, and this find really highlights that, going against stereotypes of Neanderthals as unintelligent, uncaring cavemen and cavewomen," Pomeroy said.

"If yields struggle to extend higher and dollar rallies continue to attract sellers, it will strengthen our conviction that the inflation news is largely absorbed, leaving the balance of risks tilted in favor of risk assets," said Joel Kruger, a market strategist at LMAX Group in London. Investors will also watch remarks from Fed officials including Chair Kevin Warsh at IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday for clues on the US central bank's next move.  The Australian dollar weakened 0.77 per cent to $0.6919, after local employment unexpectedly slid in September, while the Japanese yen strengthened 0.15 per cent to 158.08 per dollar.    "With the Fed entering its blackout period shortly and no tier-one data releases remaining before the meeting, market direction will likely remain driven by geopolitical uncertainty surrounding Russia/Ukraine and Iran, alongside developments in the AI story," said Shinohara.

LONDON, Oct 15 : The cost of insuring against the risk of potential US tech defaults has hit record levels, in the latest sign of credit stress building in the so-called AI trade, especially for data centre operators like CoreWeave that depend on future revenue. Although shares in companies driving the AI boom are still among the biggest gainers on global equity markets this year, many have fallen sharply in the past few weeks, as investors reassess the cost of capital against a backdrop of rising interest rates and inflation. There are also doubts among some investors and analysts about when, and in some cases, if, the billions of dollars pouring into data centres, computer power and other infrastructure will pay off. Demand for AI-linked credit default swaps (CDS), a form of insurance against default that gained prominence during the 2008 financial crisis, meanwhile has soared, even for heavyweights like Apple, Amazon and Microsoft.

For some of their more heavily indebted competitors, suppliers and customers the cost of CDS has risen even faster. WHAT IS A CDS? A derivative that provides protection against the risk that a bond issuer, whether a company or government, fails to meet its debt obligations. Bond investors expect to receive interest payments and repayment of principal when a bond matures, but they bear the risk that those payments may not be made. Buying CDS helps investors hedge that risk by effectively providing insurance against a default or other credit event. If the value of a bond drops for any reason, an investor might add to their CDS holdings to help offset that, for example. None of the companies whose CDS have risen recently have defaulted on their obligations or signalled that they may do so. IS THIS A BIG MARKET? The market for single-name CDS, which cover the bonds of a single issuer, is worth about $9 trillion, the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) said. That is a small portion of global bond markets, which have more than $150 trillion of debt securities outstanding, Bank for International Settlements data shows. The biggest CDS market is for government debt. Average daily CDS trading across the market was $16 billion in the second quarter, up from $13 billion a year earlier, the most recent data from the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation shows. Saudi Arabia is the most actively traded. But average daily trades, even for large companies, can sometimes be in the single digits, or fewer than 10 a day, meaning small transactions can have an outsized impact on prices. WHO BUYS CDS? Bond investors typically buy CDS through an intermediary, often an investment bank, which then finds a financial firm to issue an insurance policy on the bonds. These are "over-the-counter" deals that do not go through a central clearing house. Hedge funds also participate in the market, selling CDS to investors seeking to hedge exposure. The buyer pays a fee, called a premium, at regular intervals to the seller, which assumes the risk of a credit event. CDS are quoted as a credit spread, which is the number of basis points (bps) that the seller of the derivative charges the buyer for providing protection. The higher the perceived risk of a credit event, the wider the spread. A CDS quoted at 100 bps costs $1 annually to insure every $100 of debt. WHAT'S GOING ON WITH TECH CDS? CDS for CoreWeave, a heavily indebted data centre operator at the eye of the current storm, have now topped 1,100 bps for the first time, S&P Global Market Intelligence data show. They suggest a roughly 63 per cent chance of a default over the next five years, up from around 30 per cent a year ago. Tech CDS moves reflect investor concern over how quickly massive investments in AI will translate into profits, and whether heavily indebted companies can generate returns fast enough to service mounting interest costs. Oracle has seen its CDS trade at nearly 300 bps, well above those of other AI-linked companies. Nvidia CDS have also risen sharply in recent weeks to around 90 bps, Meta CDS are trading around 105 bps. By comparison, an index of investment-grade CDS is trading around 62 bps. WHAT TRIGGERS A CDS PAYOUT? A CDS pays out following a credit event, which can include a bankruptcy or a failure by an issuer to make bond payments. When concerns about an issuer's creditworthiness increase, demand for protection typically rises, widening CDS spreads. Payouts are not a given. When Swiss lender Credit Suisse collapsed and was taken over by rival UBS in 2023, the EMEA Credit Derivatives Determinations Committee (CDDC) ruled that event would not trigger a CDS payout. IF IT'S INSURANCE, WHAT'S THE PROBLEM? CDS provide a hedge for bondholders. But rising perceived risk pushes up the cost of protection, which can prompt investors to sell bonds and raise borrowing costs for issuers. That can amplify concerns about creditworthiness and potentially create a self-reinforcing cycle.

Oct 15 : Shares of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave steadied on Thursday after a sharp slump, as investors worried about the debt financing behind the artificial intelligence build-out. The loss-making cloud company has about $50 billion in debt and has become a focus of concerns that the data-center boom is being fueled by credit, straining newer players and pressuring cash flows even at giants such as Alphabet and Meta Platforms. CoreWeave's slump fueled a global rout in AI stocks, underscoring investor doubts about whether future revenue from the technology can keep pace with the spending. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company is CoreWeave's second-largest investor with about a 10 per cent stake, played down the fears. "CoreWeave’s financial strength is improving every day," Huang told reporters at a Stockholm event, adding that he does not see a need for Nvidia to backstop the company. "I'm optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing."

CoreWeave stock was last up 5 per cent after slipping as much as 8.3 per cent to its lowest level since May 2025. "The market is waking up to the fact that AI demand and a profitable business model are two very different things," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group. "It looks more like investors questioning how the build-out is being funded than a sudden collapse in appetite for AI computing. But if the cost of capital keeps rising, even strong demand may not be enough to protect the most heavily leveraged players." The jitters come as investors await Anthropic's IPO, which would be a test of whether the Claude AI model maker's rapid revenue growth can ease worries about runaway AI spending. The market selloff has already led some companies such as smart ring maker Oura to push back their listings. The yield on CoreWeave's April-issued bonds was trading around 15 per cent on Thursday, above the level that typically signals distress, drawing a "yikes" from Elon Musk on social media. The bond was last down 0.3 cents on the dollar to 79.15 cents, according to Tradeweb data. The cost of insuring its debt against default has climbed to around 1,000 basis points, implying a nearly 63 per cent chance of default in five years, up from about 30 per cent a year ago. That is despite a deal under which Nvidia will buy any unsold CoreWeave capacity through April 13, 2032. Options traders also ramped up bearish bets. Volume in put options, which give investors the right to sell shares at a certain price, hit a record high on Wednesday, according to Chris Murphy, co-head of derivatives strategy at Susquehanna. “People are using put options to hedge negative credit sentiment, and we've seen consistent and aggressive put buying all week,” Murphy said. Investors bought contracts that would profit if CoreWeave shares fell below $42.50, $50, and $60 in the coming weeks, while others used more complex trades to reduce the cost of some of those bearish wagers by taking on some risk tied to much lower share-price levels later in the year, according to Murphy and TradeAlert data. CoreWeave, which went public in March 2025, leads newer cloud providers known as neoclouds that rent out computing power from scarce and costly Nvidia processors to meet soaring demand, often borrowing heavily to buy the chips. It counts Microsoft and OpenAI among its customers, according to media reports. That leaves neoclouds exposed to any cooling in AI demand, critics have said, while the chips lose value as newer ones arrive, forcing another round of heavy spending to replace them. CoreWeave raised its annual capital spending forecast by $4 billion to as much as $39 billion in August. It is expected to post revenue of nearly $13 billion this year and a loss of $2.13 billion, according to analysts' estimates. Worries about the build-out, on which US tech giants are expected to spend more than $700 billion this year, have in recent days rippled through the stocks that have been the biggest winners since ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, a closely watched gauge of chip stocks, has erased over $1.6 trillion in market value in an 11.6 per cent slide over the past six sessions. The Nasdaq has declined more than 3 per cent in the period. On Thursday, tech shares fell across Asia, Europe and the US, dragging broader markets lower on fears that rising interest rates could hurt the sector. 'UNLIMITED' POOLS OF CAPITAL The CoreWeave selloff came as its co-founder Brannin McBee told the Financial Times that the company was seeking an investment-grade rating that would open the door to "unlimited" capital. The same day research firm Gartner said about 80 per cent of neoclouds could shut down by 2030 and that more than $3.5 trillion of AI spending could face impairment if AI providers keep up their current pace of investment. "In 2026, AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on AI infrastructure, and are forecast to invest an additional $6 trillion between 2027 and 2030," said Will Sommer, analyst at Gartner. "However, our research indicates enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures during this period." CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator pushed back on the concerns in an internal memo on Wednesday seen by Reuters, telling employees the company's deal backlog more than covers its debt obligations and that markets can sometimes "misunderstand and act irrationally".
